quizzes.lessonTitle: Final knowledge check: mixed practice across all modules
quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Final Knowledge Check

questions.questionText: A sample weighs 412.6 g wet and 356.0 g oven-dry. What is its moisture content?
questions.explanation: (412.6 − 356.0) ÷ 356.0 × 100 = 15.9%. The divisor is the oven-dry mass.

questions.questionText: What do uninsulated pins on a resistance meter report?
options: The average of the whole piece
The wettest layer that they touch
Only the wood at the tips
Only the moisture in the coating
questions.explanation: Uninsulated pins sense the lowest resistance along their length, so they report the wettest layer they touch (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: Which part of the material dominates a pinless (dielectric) reading?
questions.explanation: The field weakens rapidly with depth, so the surface layers dominate (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: To read the average moisture of a 45 mm stud that is wetter inside, set insulated pins to about:
questions.explanation: One-fifth to one-quarter of 45 mm is 9 to 11.25 mm (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: How should a plasterboard reading of 64 on a reference scale be reported?
questions.explanation: Reference-scale readings are qualitative: report points against the same material unaffected.

questions.questionText: Above what timber reading does the Wood Handbook treat meter readings as qualitative only?
questions.explanation: Readings greater than 30% must be considered only qualitative (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: What in-service moisture content range does the QBCC flood guide give for timber in houses?
questions.explanation: QBCC says timber in houses normally has an in-service moisture content of between 9% and 13%.

questions.questionText: A stud at 9 °C reads 18.0% on a resistance meter calibrated at 20 °C. What is the corrected reading?
questions.explanation: 11 °C colder: 11 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 0.98, added because the wood is cold: 19.0%.

questions.questionText: A rafter at 35 °C reads 14.0% on a meter calibrated at 20 °C. Which way does the correction go?
questions.explanation: Warm wood reads high on a resistance meter, so subtract: 15 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 1.34; 12.7%.

questions.questionText: Where should a species correction for your meter come from?
questions.explanation: Species tables are specific to each meter design; use the one supplied with your instrument.

questions.questionText: Which of these can raise a pin reading above the true moisture content?
questions.explanation: Salts and treatments raise conductivity (Wood Handbook ch. 4). Cold wood reads low, not high.

questions.questionText: Framing must be below which moisture content before relining, under the QBCC guide?
questions.explanation: Relining should wait until timber wall framing is below 16% and the framing is sound (QBCC).

questions.questionText: What does the QBCC guide call the most reliable test for dryness of a concrete floor?
questions.explanation: “For concrete floors, the most reliable test for dryness is a flooring hygrometer.” (QBCC, p. 5)

questions.questionText: A pinless scan shows vertical stripes of high readings every 450 mm on a dry wall. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Regular spacing matching stud centres points to fixings or studs; confirm with pins beside a stripe.

questions.questionText: Which daily calibration check is the weakest on its own?
questions.explanation: Two meters can be wrong in the same direction, so a meter-to-meter comparison is only a back-up.

questions.questionText: Which of these is one of the six common meter mistakes?
questions.explanation: Pins left in wet material carry moisture and contamination to the next reading.

questions.questionText: What is the dry standard for a wet plasterboard wall?
options: Same board unaffected, read same way
The meter maker’s published dry value
The highest reading on day one
questions.explanation: The dry standard is the same material, unaffected, in the same building, read the same way on the same visit.

questions.questionText: The hallway is 23 °C and 68% RH. Which EMC should dry timber there approach?
questions.explanation: Wood Handbook eq. 4-5 gives 12.5% for 23 °C, 68% RH.

questions.questionText: A laundry slab is at 16.5 °C and the room dew point is 16.8 °C. What does that mean for surface readings?
options: They prove the slab is dry
They prove moisture deep in slab
They may include some surface condensation
They need a species correction applied
questions.explanation: A surface below the dew point can collect condensation, so surface readings cannot separate it from slab moisture.

questions.questionText: Boards arrive at 13.5% for a room whose EMC is 12.0%. Under the CTIQ guidance, is acclimatisation indicated?
questions.explanation: The difference is 1.5%, inside the 2% figure in Construction timbers in Queensland; the installer still decides.
